In the first of a two-part series, physicist Milind N. Kunchur looks at the controversies around high-end audio (HEA) through the lens of how human hearing works. HEA chases fidelity with methods that can look extreme, and its claimed improvements are rarely confirmed in controlled blind tests, so skepticism abounds. Kunchur argues that some of it rests on a misunderstanding of how the time and frequency domains relate, and he explains why quick A–B blind tests can fail.

Timbre, he shows, depends heavily on time-domain detail: how each partial starts and decays, not just the average spectrum. A piano note played backwards sounds rather like a harmonica, although its spectrum is unchanged, and in K. W. Berger’s classic experiment trained musicians could no longer identify wind instruments once the attacks and decays were trimmed off. A time delay is also not a phase shift: shifting a harmonic by 90° is barely audible (Ohm’s law of acoustics), whereas delaying its onset clearly changes the sound.

Kunchur then defines temporal smearing (τ), by analogy with the blur of a telescope image. B. Leshowitz measured a transient resolution of about 4–10 μs, while the smearing of CD-quality audio (16-bit/44.1 kHz) is of the order of a sampling period. The sub-nanosecond time-shift discrimination of digital audio is not “time resolution.” A long, low-level residue can blur depth even when τ is short; both, he suggests, belong in future specifications.

Adapted into Chinese by Fanyu Meng from “Hearing and Audio: Part 1 – Frequency, Phase, and Time” by Milind N. Kunchur, published in audioXpress (March 2024). Read the original.
